impotent

IM-puh-tunt -- stress on the first syllable, IM. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Impotent is lacking the power to act or to change what is happening.

The old treaty left the council impotent: it could debate for years but could not enforce a single rule.

Example

A small town watches a river climb past every sandbag it owns, impotent to stop it: the budget is spent, the state office will not answer the phone, and the water keeps rising.

Impotent means powerless to change what is happening -- a lack of power to act, not a lack of willingness. These people want to help and simply cannot.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

powerless: Powerless is the plain, everyday statement of the fact: no power to act. Impotent is its sharper, more formal twin, and it usually carries frustration -- power that ought to exist but does not, as in an impotent committee or impotent rage.

toothless: Toothless describes a rule-maker with no way to punish or enforce -- a toothless law can be broken without cost. Impotent is broader: it means lacking the power to act at all, whether or not enforcement was ever the job. A toothless agency has rules without bite; an impotent one cannot even move.

weak: Weak means having only a little strength -- some force exists, just not much. Impotent is not a small amount of power; it is none where it counts. A weak swimmer still swims; an impotent council can meet for years and change nothing.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

potent: powerful and effective

capable: able to get things done

Where it sits · how deep the lack of power runs — ineffectual → impotent → helpless

ineffectual vs. impotent: Ineffectual is the milder charge -- an ineffectual effort has real power behind it and still fails to work -- while an impotent one had no power behind it from the very start.

helpless vs. impotent: Helpless is impotent at its most exposed: impotent says you lack the power to change things, while helpless adds that you cannot even protect yourself while they happen.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — im-

prefix — im-: not (the form in- takes before p) (Latin in-)

root — potent

root — potent: powerful, able (Latin potens 'being able, powerful,' from posse 'to be able')

Put it together

Put it together: Impotent is this unit's prefix in its im- form (in- shifts to im- before p) plus potent, a full English word meaning 'powerful.' The pair is perfectly symmetrical: potent = powerful, impotent = powerless. The same Latin posse ('to be able') also gives English possible, potential, and omnipotent.

Use the root in a new word: omnipotent

Use the root in a new word: omnipotent: In the myth, the sky god is omnipotent and can reshape the world with a single thought.

Root Check

Word Choice

Learn impotent as the mirror of potent: powerful versus powerless. In writing it attaches most often to groups, laws, and efforts -- an impotent committee, an impotent protest, an impotent threat -- and to the useful phrase 'impotent rage,' meaning anger with no power to change anything.
